Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
The night it happened, a door slamming was the sound that ended everything. Eleanor was seventy-five then, a widow of five years who had finally allowed herself to trust again. She had been a social worker for four decades, a woman who had built a career on reading people, on knowing when someone was safe. But the man she had been seeing for six months, a retired accountant named Frank, had a temper that surfaced only behind closed doors. What she remembered now, five years later, was not a sequence of events but a series of frozen images: his hand against the wall beside her head, the look in his eyes that was nothing like the man who brought her tea, the door slamming as she fled into the night. She could not put those pictures in the right order. The grief that washed over her when she recalled that moment felt as fresh as the night itself-a raw, bewildering sorrow for the woman she had been before, for the trust she had given so freely.

In the months that followed, Eleanor found herself unable to sleep. She would lie awake listening for sounds she had not noticed before: the creak of her own floorboards, the click of a lock, the distant slam of a neighbor's door. Each sound, each unexpected male voice in the grocery store line, brought back one of those frozen pictures-Frank's face, the door, the cold night air. She had come to believe that the world was not the place she had thought it was. Her beliefs about safety, about people, had been completely destroyed. She felt dirty, as though the contamination of that night had seeped into her skin. She was certain now that people could not be trusted, that her judgment had been fatally wrong. Every time a man she did not know well stood too close, or a door closed with too much force, she felt those beliefs confirmed all over again.

She began to avoid situations that brought on nightmares. She stopped napping in the afternoon, because that was when the dreams came most vividly. She tried to erase the memory entirely, pushing the images away when they surfaced, telling herself it had not happened the way she thought. She spent long hours thinking about why this had happened to her, turning over her own history like a stone, searching for the moment she had misread the signs. But the more she tried to erase the memory, the more the grief returned, and the more she felt certain that she was fundamentally contaminated. She had come to believe that her own judgment was broken, and that belief made her scan every room for exits as soon as she entered. At eighty, she still worked part-time as a social worker, but the office had become a minefield. Every male colleague who walked into her office, every client who was brought in by a male relative-she was watching the door, measuring the distance to the hallway, calculating how fast she could leave. The hypervigilance exhausted her, but she could not stop. Being superalert felt like the only thing keeping her safe.

The avoidance itself made things worse. Because she avoided the afternoon naps, she was more tired, and her mind was more prone to drift into those frozen images. Because she scanned for exits, she noticed every door that opened, and each one triggered the memory again. She had stopped visiting her son's house because his teenage son slammed his bedroom door. She had stopped going to the senior center because the men there were friendly, and friendliness now felt like a trap. Her world had shrunk to her apartment, and even there, she slept with the lights on, watching the front door. What frightened her most was not the memory itself but the feeling that she was still in that moment, still vulnerable, still unable to trust her own mind. She had come to therapy because her daughter had found her crying at the kitchen table at three in the morning, unable to explain why she was afraid to go to bed. Eleanor wanted to stop being afraid, but she was terrified that if she let go of the vigilance, something terrible would happen again.
